apollo-13.name: APOLLO 13
apollo-13.summary: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon and crippled the spacecraft. Survive the meteoroid storm, then keep an emergency lunar outpost alive!
briefing: 56 hours after launch, Oxygen Tank 2 ruptured and the Service Module lost most of its power and oxygen.
In this simulation, you fly through a meteoroid storm and crash-land near the lunar surface.
Survive the Unexpected Events and push Mission Progress to 100% to rewrite history!

cockpit.instructions: Dodge the flaming meteoroids! Every rock you avoid saves power for your outpost.

real: April 13, 1970: Oxygen Tank 2 exploded about 56 hours into the flight.
The Moon landing was cancelled. The crew squeezed into the Lunar Module 'Aquarius' and used it as a lifeboat.
Engineers on Earth built a square-to-round CO2 filter adapter out of tape, hoses and plastic bags.
Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise splashed down safely on April 17, 1970 — a 'successful failure', but no Moon science was done.
rewrite: You dodged the meteoroid storm and kept your hull strong.
You read real NASA DONKI space weather alerts and raised shields at the right moments.
You shared just 10 power units between 5 rooms and solved every emergency.
You completed 100% of the planned Moon science — the landing Apollo 13 never got to make!

mars-lander.name: MARS POLAR LANDER
mars-lander.summary: Solar flares and a descent anomaly threatened the lander. Dodge incoming solar flare plasma, then stabilize your Martian outpost!
briefing: On December 3, 1999 the Mars Polar Lander went silent just before touching down near the Martian south pole.
In this simulation, you steer through blasts of solar flare plasma and survive a rough landing.
Survive the Unexpected Events and push Mission Progress to 100% to rewrite history!

cockpit.instructions: Dodge the solar flare plasma bolts! Every blast you avoid saves power for your outpost.

real: Mars Polar Lander launched on January 3, 1999 to study water ice near the Martian south pole.
Contact was lost on December 3, 1999 during the final descent — no signal ever came back.
The most likely cause: the landing legs jolted open, and the computer mistook that bump for touchdown and shut the engine off too early.
NASA learned from it — later landers like Phoenix (2008) reached the polar region safely.
rewrite: You flew through the solar flare plasma and protected the lander's hull.
You used real NASA DONKI flare, CME and particle-storm alerts to time your shields.
You shared just 10 power units between 5 rooms and solved every Martian emergency.
You finished 100% of the polar science — the discoveries Mars Polar Lander never got to send home!
